name: Convolvulus

genus_diagnostics.habit: Trailing, prostrate, or twining herbs in the local core set.
genus_diagnostics.latex: Milky latex present in both current core species.
genus_diagnostics.leaves: Alternate, simple, commonly hastate/sagittate or lobed at the base.
genus_diagnostics.flowers: Axillary, usually 1–2 per cyme; broad funnel-shaped corolla.

quick_key.if: Plant soft-hairy/velvety; low trailing habit; leaves often broader and variably lobed; outer sepals ~7–8 mm and hairy
Plant essentially glabrous; long twining/prostrate stems; leaves narrower hastate/sagittate; sepals only ~3–4.3 mm

curation_status.visual_status: diagnostic photo polish pending; no new media acquired

look_here_first: On a flowering bindweed, turn the flower over and measure an OUTER SEPAL, then inspect its hairs. In the local two-species set, a densely hairy, cupped outer sepal about 7–7.5 mm points to C. equitans; a mostly hairless outer sepal about 3–4.5 mm points to C. arvensis. Confirm using stem/leaf hair and habit. Do not identify by flower color or arrow-shaped leaves alone.
shared_genus_traits: In this Central Texas study set, perennial trailing to twining herbs with alternate simple leaves and milky sap.
Axillary flowers with five persistent free sepals and a pleated, fused funnel/campanulate corolla; a dry capsule develops within the persistent calyx.

For genus recognition against local Ipomoea, inspect the stigma under magnification: Convolvulus has two elongated, filiform stigmas rather than Ipomoea's typically globose/capitate lobes. This is a genus-level microscope/close-up cue, not a substitute for the sepal key.

species_comparison_matrix.character: Outer sepal length (measure from base to tip)
species_comparison_matrix.equitans: 7–7.5 mm in regional Williamson County material; broad/cupped
species_comparison_matrix.arvensis: 3–4.5 mm (Flora of North America); short and elliptic
species_comparison_matrix.source: UT Convolvulus equitans treatment; FNA Convolvulus arvensis

species_comparison_matrix.arvensis: Glabrous to glabrate; some calyx/leaf variation possible

species_comparison_matrix.equitans: Stems and leaves noticeably soft-hairy to velvety/tomentose
species_comparison_matrix.arvensis: Stems usually glabrous or glabrate; leaves glabrous to occasionally puberulent beneath

species_comparison_matrix.equitans: Arrow-shaped with backward lobes; may be broader or irregularly lobed
species_comparison_matrix.arvensis: Usually narrow hastate/sagittate, but leaf blades range elliptic to ovate-lanceolate

species_comparison_matrix.equitans: Often low, prostrate to decumbent and several-stemmed at base
species_comparison_matrix.arvensis: Long trailing or twining branches, often climbing; rhizomatous persistent perennial
species_comparison_matrix.weight: SUPPORTING; both can trail and both are perennial

species_comparison_matrix.equitans: About 15 mm long, ca. 20 mm across in local description

quick_comparison_steps: First confirm Convolvulaceae: alternate leaves, five free persistent sepals and a pleated fused corolla.
Turn an open flower sideways; use a millimeter ruler on an outer sepal (not a bract).
Check the same sepal under a 10× lens for dense hairs versus a nearly bare surface.
Compare hairs on stems and leaf undersides at multiple nodes, then use leaf base and growth form only as supporting evidence.
If the flower is gone or the measurements conflict, retain Convolvulus sp. rather than forcing a species; seek fruiting/flowering material.
overlap_and_cautions: C. equitans and C. arvensis can both be perennial, arrow-leaved and trailing. Leaf outline, vine length and white/pink corolla color cannot reliably split them.
FNA records some abaxial puberulence in C. arvensis; absence/presence of hairs on a single leaf is weaker than outer sepal length plus calyx hairs.
The 7–7.5 mm C. equitans measurement comes from a Williamson County treatment, not a full geographic range; verify on several flowers when possible.
C. arvensis is an introduced comparison/encounter species; inclusion does not certify it as target-zone native. Do not reopen or change existing species range metadata.
A large bract enclosing the calyx suggests Calystegia rather than these Convolvulus; an Ipomoea with a similar flower can be checked by its generally globose stigma lobes and species-specific sepals.

local_lookalikes.name: Ipomoea hederacea
local_lookalikes.separate_by: Usually lobed/ivy-like leaves and species-specific long-pointed hairy sepals; inspect globose stigma lobes vs two filiform Convolvulus stigmas; do not use flower color.

local_lookalikes.name: Ipomoea cordatotriloba
local_lookalikes.separate_by: Often broader heart-shaped to three-lobed leaves, but overlap requires examining sepals and the usually globose Ipomoea stigma.

local_lookalikes.name: Calystegia spp.
local_lookalikes.relationship: regional genus-level comparison; only where actually encountered
local_lookalikes.separate_by: Two large foliaceous bracteoles immediately below and partly concealing the calyx; Convolvulus has smaller bracts set farther below.
